chunks: Three [narrators] - Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father and Muhammad ibn Isma'il from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, all from Hammad ibn Isa from Hariz from Zurarah, who said:

I was sitting with Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) one day when a man came to him and entered. He said to him, 'May I be your ransom, I am a man whose mosque is with my people. If I do not pray with them, they will speak ill of me and say such and such.' He said, 'If you say that, indeed Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said: Whoever hears the call to prayer and does not respond to it without an excuse, he has no prayer.'
The man left, and he said to him, 'Do not leave praying with them, and behind every Imam.'
When he left, I said to him, 'May I be your ransom, your saying to this man when he asked you seemed heavy upon me, if they are not believers?'
He smiled (peace be upon him) and said, 'I do not see you except here, O Zurarah. What excuse do you want that is greater than the fact that he is prayed behind?'
Then he said, 'O Zurarah, what do you think?' I said, 'Pray in your mosques and pray with your Imams.'
ai.seo_question: Should a Muslim pray in congregation with non-believers or sinners?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Shia principle of *al-istihna'* (exclusion) from the congregation, where the Imam advises Zurarah to pray with the non-believers to avoid social friction, citing the Prophet's statement that hearing the call without excuse invalidates one's prayer. The Imam’s laughter and subsequent clarification highlight that the validity of the prayer depends on the Imam's status rather than the congregation's, emphasizing communal unity (*jamāʿah*) as a practical necessity for the faithful living among non-Shias.
